slides.headline: Roughly 4 months without a single meal.
slides.sub: How a male emperor penguin keeps one egg alive on the Antarctic ice

slides.headline: One egg, handed straight over
slides.body: The female lays a single egg just before winter and passes it to her mate almost immediately. Then she leaves for the sea.

slides.headline: He holds it on his feet
slides.body: The male keeps the egg on top of his feet, under a fold of skin called the brood pouch, for roughly 65 days.

slides.label: winter temperatures routinely dip below this
slides.body: Incubation lasts 60–68 days through gale-force winds. With no access to food, the male lives off his fat reserves.

slides.headline: Huddling saves energy
slides.body: Huddles can hold fewer than 200 birds or as many as 5,000 to 6,000. Packing together conserves energy and lets them fast for longer.

slides.label: of his body mass, roughly, lost over the fast
slides.body: If the chick hatches before the female returns, he feeds it a milky secretion. After roughly 4 months he goes back to sea.

slides.headline: Send this to the most patient parent you know.
slides.body: Survival stories, straight from the sources. Follow @earthspirit_nature.

caption:
A male emperor penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri) fasts for roughly 4 months to keep one egg warm through the Antarctic winter.

While he waits, the female travels some 80 to 160 km from the colony to the sea to feed. To lose less heat he stands on just his heels and tail, so the soles of his feet stay off the ice. Chicks hatch in August, when the females come back to take over.

Swipe to see how he gets through it. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Animal Diversity Web; Britannica.
